papers.title: Foliar and floral frost damage reshape reproductive phenology with limited carry-over effects
papers.abstract: Abstract Late spring frost is an intensifying climatic disturbance, yet how frost damage to different organs (leaves and flowers) reshapes reproductive phenology and generates carry-over effects remains unclear. Using 259,732 phenological observations across eight European woody species spanning 1950–2024, we show that foliar frost damage shortened the fruit development period (FDP; the interval from flowering to fruit maturity) by 1.6 days, driven by delayed flowering and advanced fruit maturity. Conversely, floral frost damage prolonged FDP by 1.3 days through delayed fruit maturity, with both effects strengthening under greater frost severity. Accounting for anomalously warm conditions in the frost year substantially reduced the estimated delays in flowering and subsequent-year phenology, indicating that neglecting climatic context leads to overestimation of frost effects. These findings reveal organ-specific pathways through which frost damage reshapes reproductive phenology while generating limited carry-over effects, refining current understanding of phenological responses under climate change.

papers.title: The Plant Cell welcomes 2027 Assistant Features Editors
Biosynthesis of iboga alkaloids
papers.abstract: Abstract Tabernanthe iboga (iboga) is the source of voacangine, which is widely used as a semi-synthetic starting material for the anti-addiction agent ibogaine. Despite extensive investigation of voacangine biosynthesis, production of this compound cannot be reconstituted in a heterologous host, suggesting that one or more enzymes required for biosynthesis are missing. Additionally, T. iboga produces ibophyllidine, a pyrroloindole alkaloid that utilizes the same upstream precursor as voacangine, but is a member of a structurally distinct alkaloid class. Here we use bulk and single cell gene expression from leaf and root tissue to identify the unknown enzymes from these two pathways. We identify two additional enzymes that enable biosynthesis of voacangine in a heterologous host. The missing enzymes includes a pathogenesis-related (PR)10 family protein that likely catalyzes cyclization of a transient intermediate. Careful analysis of gene expression profiles in leaf and root also enabled the discovery of four additional enzymes that convert an upstream intermediate to ibophyllidine. This work reveals the chemical logic that generates two distinct alkaloid scaffolds in this important medicinal plant.

papers.title: Dual Pathways Mediate Blue Light Signaling-Regulated Melatonin Accumulation in Tomato Fruits
papers.abstract: Abstract Melatonin is an antioxidant and growth regulator in plants that directly or indirectly influences the yield and quality of vegetable crops. Melatonin accumulation is highly sensitive to light signals. Nevertheless, the biosynthetic route responsible for light response, along with its underlying regulatory architecture, remains elusive. Here, we demonstrate that blue light stimulates the expression of SlASMT7, which encodes an enzyme in the "serotonin–5-methoxytryptamine" melatonin biosynthetic pathway, while also repressing melatonin catabolism via SlM2H. Both effects are mediated by the transcription factor SlHY5. SlHY5 activates SlASMT7 by directly binding to its promoter, whereas it represses SlM2H expression by recruiting histone deacetylases SlHDA4 and SlHDA8. Melatonin accumulation is temporally phased—biosynthesis predominates at the breaker stage, whereas SlM2H-mediated catabolism drives its decline and is accompanied by a stage-dependent metabolic transition. The HY5–ASMT7–M2H module shows consistent directional trends across multiple fleshy fruit species, suggesting possible evolutionary conservation. Together, these findings define a blue light-regulated pathway that links transcriptional and epigenetic control to melatonin homeostasis and metabolic reprogramming, providing a molecular framework for improving fruit quality through breeding and light management.

papers.title: A Super-Enhancer-Like Element and a Positive Feedback Loop Drive Ultra-High Expression of CCS for Red Pepper Ripening
papers.abstract: Abstract The capsanthin-capsorubin synthase (CCS) gene drives red pigment accumulation in pepper fruit through a ripening-specific transcriptional surge. In the pericarp of mature fruit, it is the second most highly expressed gene; however, the regulatory basis for this exceptional activation remains poorly understood. Here, we identified a super-enhancer-like (SE-like) element in the pepper (Capsicum annuum) CCS gene (CaCCS) promoter, composed of 22 tandem repeats partitioned into three groups by two intervening miniature inverted-repeat transposable elements (MITEs) insertions. MITE-associated siRNAs and DNA methylation suggest a potential role for these insertions in CaCCS repression before ripening, whereas CaDML2-mediated demethylation alleviates promoter repression during ripening. CArG-box motifs present in all repeats mediate CaRIN–CaTAGL1 activation of CaCCS in a copy number-dependent manner. Mechanistically, CaRIN binds and stabilizes CaTAGL1, and the resulting heteromeric complex activates the CaRIN promoter, establishing an autoregulatory positive feedback loop that amplifies CaRIN accumulation during ripening. CaRIN further undergoes liquid–liquid phase separation through its C-terminal intrinsically disordered region, forming nuclear condensates that are enriched at the CaCCS promoter and contain CaTAGL1. This study reveals how an SE-like cis-element, MITEs-directed epigenetic dynamics, and a self-reinforcing CaRIN–CaTAGL1 transcriptional circuit and biomolecular condensates work together to drive the ripening-specific increase in CaCCS expression. Our findings reveal the regulatory mechanisms through which quantitative and temporal control of gene expression underlies metabolic innovation in Capsicum species.

papers.title: Steering nanometric reductive-oxidative Fenton-like cycle for PFAS mineralization
papers.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs), known as “forever chemicals,” have highly stable C─F bonds that render them resistant to destruction by conventional water treatment processes. Here, we developed a destructive technology that does not require external photo-, electro-, or heat energy input, relying simply on Fenton-like cycles (peroxymonosulfate activation) under nanometric spatial confinement. Unlike the ordinary activation process, confinement shielded peroxymonosulfate radicals ( S O 5 • − ) from external quenching and enabled them to remain active for reductive defluorination. Coupled with oxidative sulfate radicals ( S O 4 • − ), this process unlocked a synergistic “reduction-oxidation” destruction pathway. Specifically, the catalyst was designed by planting single-atom cobalt on MXene nanosheets, whose interlaminar confinement directed efficient PFAS mineralization via alternating α-carbon defluorination (by S O 5 • − ) and decarbonization (by S O 4 • − ). We further constructed a Fenton bed that allowed highly efficient and cost-effective treatment of PFASs in complex water matrices. Our findings underscore the promising potential of nanoconfinement in driving reductive-oxidative Fenton-like cycles toward efficient PFAS mineralization.

papers.title: Soybean Pb encodes a WD40 protein regulating pubescence tip morphology and seed size during domestication
Impacts of medications for obesity on global health and the environment
papers.abstract: Abstract A new generation of medications for obesity could transform the global food system. While research has explored their health impacts, their implications for global food demand and land use remain unquantified. We apply a global food system model to project the impact of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1) uptake to 2050 among people with obesity under two scenarios: reduced calorie intake while maintaining dietary composition, and reduced calorie intake combined with shifts towards the EAT–Lancet diet. Compared with the Reference scenario, GLP-1-mediated calorie reduction alone results in up to 6.6 million avoided deaths globally in 2050 and 32 Mha more natural land area, reflecting reductions in cropland, pasture and managed forest. Combining GLP-1 use with EAT–Lancet dietary shifts increases these estimates to 7.7 million avoided deaths and 46 Mha more natural land. Lower food prices increase food consumption among untreated populations, including unhealthy foods, partially offsetting these gains.

papers.title: Cool nights attenuate morning OsRLCK309 expression and compromise blast resistance in rice
papers.abstract: Abstract Nighttime cooling during day-night thermocycles has long been associated with increased rice blast severity, yet the host mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that cool-night pre-exposure weakens subsequent blast resistance in rice under a common post-inoculation regime and is associated with reduced morning expression of a receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase (RLCK)-enriched gene set. We identify OsRLCK309, a cool-night-responsive receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase, as a positive regulator of blast resistance and pattern-triggered immunity (PTI), including chitin-induced reactive oxygen species production, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) activation, and Ca2+ influx. OsRLCK309 associates with the chitin co-receptor kinase CHITIN ELICITOR RECEPTOR KINASE 1 (OsCERK1), and OsCERK1-mediated phosphorylation of OsRLCK309 at Ser245 and Thr246 contributes to full activation of defense against rice blast. Under warm nights, CIRCADIAN CLOCK ASSOCIATED 1 (OsCCA1) promotes a morning-phased expression peak of OsRLCK309. Cool nights attenuate this OsCCA1-associated morning peak and induce dehydration-responsive element-binding protein 1A (OsDREB1A), which activates the OsRLCK309 promoter and contributes to its nighttime induction under cool-night conditions. In transgenic complementation lines, mutation of the two OsDREB1A-binding sites in the OsRLCK309 promoter attenuated cool-night-responsive transcriptional redistribution and was associated with reduced disease severity after cool-night pre-exposure, with minimal detectable agronomic trade-offs under our conditions. These results support a thermocycle-sensitive model linking night-temperature history to transcriptional timing, receptor-proximal immune signaling, and blast disease in rice, and suggest that modification of the DREB-binding motifs in the OsRLCK309 promoter may help maintain blast resistance under variable night temperatures.

papers.title: Reexamining the transcriptional landscape of plant specialized metabolism: from a hierarchical to a multi-layered and flatter regulatory model
papers.abstract: Abstract Plant specialized metabolites are essential mediators of adaptation to dynamic environmental conditions, functioning in defense, signaling, and developmental regulation. Traditionally, the regulation of plant specialized metabolism has been conceptualized through a hierarchical framework where global regulators dictate developmental cues which control downstream pathway-specific transcription factors (TFs) to activate individual biosynthetic pathways. In this model, primary metabolism is often considered a disconnected precursor supplier. Emerging genome-wide evidence has increasingly challenged this linear paradigm, revealing an underappreciated level of cross-talk and metabolic coordination. Regulatory networks exist on a quantitative spectrum from the linear hierarchical to highly decentralized flatter networks with extensive connections between both regulatory layers and input signals. This review synthesizes recent advances that suggest a shift in evidence indicating that a better regulatory model for specialized metabolism might be on the decentralized, "flatter" regulatory network architecture end of this spectrum. In this flatter model, individual TFs simultaneously target diverse promoter loci across multiple metabolic layers, while individual enzyme promoters are conversely targeted by a multitude of TFs. This integrated framework is exemplified by developing research spanning diverse classes of specialized metabolites, including glucosinolates, phenylpropanoids, and terpenoids. Focusing on these pathways, we discuss how flat TF networks simultaneously regulate precursor allocation, specialized metabolite production, and stress responsiveness, thereby linking primary and specialized metabolism into cohesive regulatory modules. Collectively, these findings suggest a shift from exclusively hierarchical models toward a flatter and distributed regulatory perspective that better reflects the precise signal-processing capacity and combinatorial control of plant metabolic regulation.

papers.title: Nutritional niches reveal mutualism resilience in urban fungus-farming ants
papers.abstract: Maintaining optimized nutrient exchange between partnered species across changing environments presents a fundamental challenge for nutritional mutualisms. Yet quantitative approaches linking nutrient acquisition by one partner with the nutritional requirements of the other have been lacking. Here we extend the Nutritional Geometry Framework from organisms and colonies to interspecific mutualisms by linking realized nutritional niches (RNNs) with nutritional performance landscapes to quantify nutritional homeostasis between interacting species. Nutritional analyses of thousands of DNA-barcoded plant fragments collected by free-ranging Panamanian leafcutter ants revealed that RNNs for fungal cultivar provisioning diverged between degraded urban and intact rainforest habitats. Despite this, colonies converged on similar nutritional intake targets that were similarly positioned relative to regions of high fungal performance, while fungal nutritional yield remained stable across habitats. These findings demonstrate that correspondence between colony nutritional intake and fungal nutritional performance provides a quantitative means of assessing nutritional homeostasis across interacting species and establishes a foundation for comparative analyses of nutrient exchange across mutualisms experiencing environmental change.

papers.title: Structural insights into inhibition and activation mechanisms of plant calcium-dependent protein kinases
papers.abstract: Calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) comprise the major group of Ca 2+ -regulated kinases in plants and protists. These enzymes comprise an N-terminal kinase domain and a C-terminal Ca 2+ -dependent activation domain (CAD). We solved the crystal structures of autoinhibited and activated forms of a plant CDPK, Arabidopsis CPK3. In the autoinhibited form, the CAD resembles a “dumbbell-like” calmodulin protein with a long helix in the N terminus that inhibits the kinase domain in a pseudo-substrate manner. Upon Ca 2+ binding to the four EF-hands, CAD undergoes a dramatic conformational change with a rotation around the kinase domain, thus exposing its active site for substrate recognition. Our structural and biochemical studies reveal that most plant CDPKs may involve distinct mechanisms of activation compared with CDPKs from the apicomplexan parasites.

papers.title: Competitive disruption of COI1 receptor assembly by a hemibiotrophic bacterial effector suppresses jasmonate-mediated immunity
papers.abstract: Hormone pathways are central hubs in plant immunity, and their receptors, the critical initiators of signaling cascades, are logical targets of pathogen effectors. The jasmonic acid (JA) pathway is a cornerstone of defense against phytopathogens, especially necrotrophs. However, whether pathogens can directly target its receptor COI1 to subvert this defense layer has remained unclear. Here, we show that JA signaling positively regulates resistance to the devastating hemibiotrophic pathogen Ralstonia solanacearum and identified a bacterial effector, RipBO, that directly targets COI1 to counteract this defense. RipBO binds with high affinity to the F-box domain of COI1, competitively disrupts the COI1-ASK interaction, and thereby blocks SCF COI1 complex assembly. This disruption effectively stabilizes JAZ repressors and paralyzes JA-mediated immunity. Our findings clarify the contribution of JA signaling to bacterial wilt resistance and identify direct targeting of the hormone receptor as a pathogen virulence strategy, pointing to a potential vulnerability for crop protection.

papers.title: Tandem duplication of oxidosqualene cyclases and enzyme promiscuity of cytochromes P450 contribute to the diversity of triterpenoids in Eleutherococcus senticosus
papers.abstract: Abstract Triterpenoid saponins in Araliaceae plants exhibit remarkable structural diversity, with species-specific compounds like ginsenosides and ciwujianosides, yet the genetic basis remains elusive. Here, we report a chromosome-scale genome assembly of Eleutherococcus senticosus (Rupr. & Maxim.) Maxim. (1.39 Gb, 51,243 genes) and demonstrate that it shares a lineage-specific whole-genome duplication (WGD-α, Ks = 0.112) with Hedera helix. Phylogenomic analyses reveal a 4:4 syntenic relationship between these species, confirming their close evolutionary relationship. Notably, both E. senticosus and H. helix lack the dammarenediol-II synthase (DDS) gene, explaining the absence of ginsenoside-type saponins. Through genome mining and functional validation, we identify eight OSC genes, including a tandemly duplicated cluster on chromosome 18 unique to E. senticosus. Biochemical assays show that EsOSC4 and EsOSC12 synthesize tirucalla-7,24-dien-3β-ol, representing the first enzymatic characterization of a tirucallane synthase in Araliaceae, while EsOSC13 produces lupeol. Site-directed mutagenesis establishes residue 372 (valine in EsOSC13, methionine in EsOSC4/12) as critical for this functional divergence. Moreover, we discover three promiscuous CYP716 enzymes (EsCYP716A244/A450/A452) capable of oxidizing β-amyrin, lupeol, and tirucalla-7,24-dien-3β-ol at multiple positions, generating diverse oxidized derivatives. These findings reveal tandem duplication and enzyme promiscuity as primary mechanisms driving triterpenoid diversity in E. senticosus, with implications for synthetic biology applications in saponin production.
